newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya trade wants coffee auctions, growers waver.
newsitem.headline: Kenya trade wants coffee auctions, growers waver.

text.p: Coffee traders fully back the existing auctions system in the debate on market liberalisation in Kenya, but farmers are less sure.
John Kyendo, one of Kenya's 300,000 smallholders, said farmers were pulled towards private treaty sales by the lure of ready cash on delivery of their coffee beans.

"When you deliver coffee to the cooperative, you wait until it is auctioned to be paid. These people (private treaty) offer you ready cash. Small growers are peasants who need the money," Kyendo told Reuters.

"Right now a majority of farmers are deeply confused. The auctions give us the best prices but we have to wait for the money. Private treaty may give us a raw deal but there is ready cash," Kyendo added.
The Coffee Board of Kenya and major trade houses say the auctions are what local dealers and foreign buyers want, are known as reliable around the world and have been run smoothly.
They argue that any changes would disrupt the market and undermine global confidence in the quality of Kenyan coffee.
"We prefer that all coffee be sold through the auctions," said a senior trader.

"Private treaty sales we are very much against because they lack transparency and could undermine farm prices and quality in the long term," added the trader, speaking to Reuters in this key growing town 80 km north of Nairobi.

The government, acting on a report prepared by the industry, this month said coffee would only be sold via the single weekly auction. It also put in place measures to strengthen the Coffee Board of Kenya as sole marketing agency.

But Pius Ngugi, a farmer and chairman of the Thika Coffee Mills, said the Coffee Board should relinquish its "monopoly-like" marketing role and allow roasters direct access to farmers to negotiate prices.
Ngugi saw such an arrangement as cutting red-tape and ending delays often experienced in passing money down to farmers after the auction or from what he saw as "middlemen deductions".
But an official at a leading coffee house said traders joined the board long ago in rejecting private treaty sales.

"Some (Kenyan) millers want direct contact with roasters who sign for a price and quantity for the whole season. Auctions react to the world situation, so farmers get the best of the world each time they offer (for sale)," the official said.

"Private treaty sales will mean big losses and the farmers will suffer. We traders are between roasters and the farmers, we are paying the farmers' price. Roasters do not necessarily look at farmer needs, they look at their own."
